tier_reason: First-party wiki case study (benchmarks_php) comparing a CppCMS blog with WordPress 2.5 plus a patched WP-Cache-2 on an AMD Athlon XP 64bit with 1 GB RAM; no compiler or flags and no benchmark code in the repo. cppcms.com is EGRESS_BLOCKED here, so numbers were checked against WebSearch summaries only (snippet only), which caps it at C.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Snippet only (cppcms.com blocked). benchmarks_php, no cache: CppCMS 310 fetches/s vs WordPress 7.6 fetches/s, about 41x (derived from page data); warm-up 0.28 s vs 13.0 s. Cache miss-ratio table (fetches/s, CppCMS vs WordPress): 0% 2300 vs 711 (about 3.2x, derived); 3% 1940 vs 176 (about 11x, derived; the page states 'more than 10 times' at 3%); 40% 570 vs 13 (about 44x, derived). The page's own wording is that PHP performance drops very fast once the miss ratio reaches a few percent. Separate case study benchmarks_all (CppCMS 0.99.3 vs PHP 5.2.6 on lighttpd/FastCGI, Mono 2.6.7 Asp.Net, JSP on Tomcat 6.0.18): at 0% miss CppCMS 3200.73 req/s vs PHP 974.142, JSP/Tomcat 821.887, Mono 747.164 (about 3.3x-4.3x, derived from page data); PHP used almost 3x and Java Servlets almost 30x the memory of CppCMS.
corrections.caveats: SNIPPET ONLY: cppcms.com and blog.cppcms.com are blocked by the egress proxy, so benchmarks_php and benchmarks_all were never opened; figures come from WebSearch result summaries. The summaries disagree: one printed WordPress 71 fetches/s at 0% miss and a scaled-down column (37, 17, 11 ...), another printed 71 at 0% followed by 370 at 1%, 176 at 3%, 118 at 5%; 711 at 0% is the reading consistent with the 1% row and with the page's 'more than 10 times at 3%' statement (1940/176), but it was not seen on the page. Both summaries print identical 40% and 50% rows (570 vs 13), so the 50% row is uncertain and only the 40% row is used. One earlier summary printed 3,100 fetches/s for the no-cache CppCMS figure; 310 repeated in two summaries. First-party, roughly 2008-2010 era numbers (WordPress 2.5, PHP 5, Athlon XP 64) comparing two different blog applications, not a controlled framework microbenchmark; the PHP side is WordPress with a WP-Cache-2 plugin patched by the author. The earlier claim that the CppCMS blog beats JSP and PHP blogs by an order of magnitude was not supported by the summaries: the benchmarks_all case study shows about 3.3x-4.3x at 0% miss and says the C#, Java and PHP implementations behaved similarly; the order-of-magnitude statement there concerns memory (Java/Tomcat and Mono). The record's lighttpd 1.4.13 and MySQL 5.0 versions were not seen in any summary (benchmarks_all names PHP 5.2.6 with lighttpd and FastCGI). Compiler, flags and benchmark code (the blog application) are not in the CppCMS repo. The 'LGPLv3' tag in the awesome-cpp list is outdated: README and COPYING.TXT say MIT since 1.2. Baseline is a PHP application, not a C++ incumbent. Cap at C.

notes: Real, maintained project (MIT, 528 stars, last commit 2025-12-18). Shortcomings: snippet-only evidence because cppcms.com is blocked; first-party, ~2008-era, app-vs-app comparison with a PHP baseline, no compiler/flags/code; summaries disagree on the WordPress 0% miss value (71 vs 711) and the order-of-magnitude claim over JSP/PHP was not supported (benchmarks_all shows about 3.3x-4.3x at 0% miss). claimed_speedup and caveats rewritten accordingly.

tier_reason: First-party wiki page (ENG-14-Benchmarks) states CPU (2x Xeon E5-2670), OS and gcc 7.3.0 and the Drogon side code is public (examples/benchmark/BenchmarkCtrl.cc), but optimisation flags are not stated and the nginx hello_world module and config are not published, so not A; no independent source was opened.

corrections.caveats: First-party wiki page (WebFetch reports it last revised 2024-08-06); the Drogon side is in the repo (examples/benchmark/BenchmarkCtrl.h and BenchmarkCtrl.cc: HttpSimpleController on /benchmark) but the nginx hello_world module and nginx configuration are not published, compiler optimisation flags and build type are not stated, and the placement of the httpress client (same host or not) is not stated. BenchmarkCtrl calls resp->setExpiredTime(0), so Drogon serves a framework-cached, pre-rendered response; the current examples/benchmark/main.cc no longer matches the wiki setup (it registers a sync advice on '/' and uses setThreadNum(0)). Nginx is run through a hand-written module rather than serving a static file, which is not the usual nginx deployment. The no-keep-alive 100-connection row was run with httpress -t 12 while the other rows used -t 16, and its nginx figure is inconsistent (31/49, max below min). Environment is CentOS 7.4 and gcc 7.3.0, so numbers are several years old. The author writes 'If someone does a more accurate test, please correct me.' The README links the TechEmpower Framework Benchmarks results; techempower.com was not opened, so that independent evidence is not used for the tier (it could lift the entry to B in a session that can reach it, if it shows a win over nginx). The repo has moved to drogonframework/drogon; an-tao/drogon still resolves there.

notes: All six kQPS rows match the wiki page exactly; derived ratios (about 1.6x-1.7x keep-alive, about 2.9x-4.5x without) are correctly labelled. Shortcomings: first-party hello-world test, nginx module/config unpublished, flags unstated, Drogon response cached via setExpiredTime(0), mismatched -t 12 in one row, inconsistent nginx 31/49 figure. Metadata confirmed (MIT, 14.3k stars, last commit 2026-10-06, not archived, not a fork).
